title: Getting ready for the first day of preschool
summary: Small, simple steps that help a young child, and their parents, feel ready for a happy start at preschool.
coverAlt: Two children working together at a classroom table
intro: The first day of preschool is a big step for a little person, and often for their parents too. A few small routines in the weeks before can turn nervous excitement into a confident start.

sections.heading: Talk about it, cheerfully
sections.text: Mention preschool now and then in everyday chat: the friends your child will meet, the songs they will sing and the toys they will play with. Keep it light and positive, and answer questions simply and honestly.

sections.heading: Practise the new routine
sections.text:
A week or two before school starts, move bedtime and wake-up time to match the school day. Try a short morning rehearsal: breakfast, getting dressed and leaving the house at the same time each day.

- Pack the school bag together the night before
- Let your child choose their water bottle or lunch box
- Keep mornings calm and unhurried
sections.caption: A bright, open space to explore helps new children feel at home.

sections.heading: Keep goodbyes short and warm
sections.text: A hug, a clear goodbye and a promise of when you will be back works better than slipping away. Children settle faster when they know what to expect, and teachers are used to helping with first-day tears.

sections.heading: Celebrate the small wins
sections.text: Ask about the day with open questions such as **“What made you smile today?”** and celebrate every small step, from saying hello to a new friend to trying a new activity.

quote.text: Children settle faster when they know what to expect.

takeaways: Talk about preschool positively and often
Start the school-day routine a week or two early
Say a short, warm goodbye and come back on time

title: Why play is serious learning
summary: Children under five learn best by seeing and doing. Here is what is really happening when a preschooler plays.
coverAlt: A bright indoor play area with rockers and slides on green turf
intro: To a grown-up, it can look like a child is simply playing. Look closer and you will see a scientist testing ideas, an engineer building, a storyteller practising new words and a team player learning to take turns.

sections.heading: Learning through the senses
sections.text: Children under five understand the world best through what they see, touch and do. Hands-on Montessori materials let them learn through their senses, at their own pace, and what they learn this way stays with them.
sections.caption: Picture cards turn new words into something children can see and hold.

sections.heading: Big skills from small games
sections.text: Stacking blocks builds early maths and patience. Pretend play builds language and empathy. Group games build problem-solving, communication and teamwork, the real-life skills that prepare children for what comes next.

sections.heading: Moving bodies, growing minds
sections.text: Movement matters too. Dance, yoga and outdoor play strengthen the body, improve balance and coordination, and help children focus when it is time to sit and listen.
sections.caption: Yoga and movement help little bodies and minds find their balance.

sections.heading: How to play along at home
sections.text: You don’t need special toys. Follow your child’s interests, ask open questions (“What happens if…?”), and give them time to try things their own way before stepping in.

quote.text: Children under five learn best by seeing and doing.

title: Five simple ways to build a love of reading at home
summary: Reading together for a few minutes a day does more than any app. Five easy habits that make books a favourite part of the day.
coverAlt: A teacher showing a picture card to a group of children
intro: A love of reading starts long before a child can read on their own. These five habits take only a few minutes a day.

sections.heading: Make it a daily ritual
sections.text: Pick a regular time, such as after dinner or just before bed, and read together every day, even if only for five minutes.

sections.heading: Let your child choose
sections.text: Children read more when they pick the book. Read the same favourite again and again; repetition builds vocabulary and confidence.

sections.heading: Talk about the pictures
sections.text: Point, ask and wonder together: “What do you think happens next?” “How does the bear feel?” Talking about a story matters as much as reading the words.

sections.heading: Keep books within reach
sections.text: A low shelf or a basket of books in the living room invites children to pick one up on their own.

sections.heading: Be a reading role model
sections.text: When children see the grown-ups around them reading, they learn that books are for everyone, not just for school.

takeaways: Read together every day, even briefly
Let your child choose (and repeat) favourites
Talk about the story and the pictures
Keep books where little hands can reach them

title: A note to our parents
summary: Thank you for trusting us with your children. A few words on what we believe in and how we work with families.
coverAlt: Children practising yoga together in a bright hall
intro:
Dear parents,

Thank you for trusting us with the most precious part of your life. Every morning, when your child walks through our doors, we take that trust seriously.

sections.text: We believe every child is special. We embrace diversity and make sure every child feels valued and included, whatever their background or ability, and we set achievable goals for each child and celebrate every milestone, big or small.

We also believe in working together with you. We are open and honest with families, and we would love to hear from you, whether it is a question, an idea or simply a story from home about something your child learned.
